title: POTA — Live Spots and Self-Spotting
subtitle: See who's on the air right now for Parks on the Air, look up park information, and — when you're activating — post your own spot so chasers can find you, all with one manual press.
in_this_chapter: What POTA is and what this feature does
Viewing live spots and park information
Self-spotting: putting yourself on the map
The good-citizen rules the program follows
That no login is needed (and what is separate)

callout.label: QUICK VERSION
callout.text: The **POTA** tab shows a live list of activators on the air right now. When you're the one activating, fill in your park and frequency and press **Spot me** to post yourself so chasers can find you. One press posts one spot — nothing happens in the background, and you never need to log in.

blocks.h1: What This Is / What It Is For

blocks.p: **Parks on the Air (POTA)** is a popular program where operators ("activators") set up in a public park and make contacts, while "chasers" try to work them. A live **spotting** website shows who's on the air, where, and on what frequency. Activation Planner connects to POTA so you can both **see the spots** and, when you're activating, **spot yourself** so chasers know you're there.

callout.label: JARGON, IN PLAIN WORDS
callout.text: **Spot:** a short public post saying "this operator is on the air at this park, on this frequency, right now." **Self-spot:** posting a spot for *yourself* when you're the activator, so chasers can find and work you.

blocks.h1: Viewing Live Spots and Park Info

blocks.p: Open the **POTA** tab to see the current spots — activators on the air now, with their callsign, park, frequency, and mode. You can also look up park information. This part is purely read-only: you're just viewing public information that POTA already publishes, which is handy for finding someone to contact or checking whether a park is already being activated.

blocks.h1: Self-Spotting — Putting Yourself on the Map

blocks.p: When **you** are the activator, self-spotting posts you to the live list so chasers can find you — especially valuable in a quiet park or on a band where nobody would stumble across you otherwise.

steps: Enter the **park** you're activating and the **frequency** and **mode** you're on.
Your spot appears on the public POTA list. Press it again later (for example, when you change bands) to post an updated spot.

callout.label: ONE PRESS = ONE SPOT
callout.text: Self-spotting is always a deliberate, manual action. The program never spots you automatically or in the background — it posts exactly once, each time you press the button, and only for you.

blocks.h1: The Good-Citizen Rules the Program Follows

blocks.p: POTA's spotting service is shared by the whole community, so Activation Planner is deliberately built to be a considerate guest on it. The program:

bullets: **Only spots you** — it will never spot another operator. (The person spotting and the person being spotted are always the same: you.)
**Only spots when you press the button** — no automatic, scheduled, or bulk spotting.
**Identifies itself honestly** — each spot is tagged as coming from "Activation Planner" so POTA can see where it originated.

blocks.p: These constraints keep the feature useful to you without putting extra load on, or misusing, a community service.

Both viewing spots and self-spotting work **without any account or password** — they use POTA's open spotting service, so there's nothing to sign into. The only POTA activity that requires a login is **uploading your logs for award credit**, which is a completely separate task and is **not** something Activation Planner does. This program is a *planning and spotting* tool, not a logger.

callout.label: LOGGING STAYS ELSEWHERE
callout.text: Activation Planner intentionally doesn't log your contacts — keep using your normal logging program for that. This tool helps you plan the activation and spot yourself; recording and submitting QSOs is a job for a dedicated logger.

rows: Check your internet connection (a hotspot is fine). The spot list comes from POTA's online service.
Confirm you're online, that the park and frequency are filled in, and press **Spot me** again. Each press posts one spot.
It asked me to log in
It shouldn't — spotting needs no login. If you hit a login prompt, that's for a separate service (like log upload), which this program doesn't do.
I changed bands and my spot is stale
Post a fresh spot with your new frequency by pressing **Spot me** again.
No — the program only ever spots you (self-spot only), by design. Your friend can spot themselves from their own setup.
